CHAIR ROBERT HOLDEN PRESIDING

June 10, 2025

Chair Holden and members of the New York City Council Committee on Veterans. Thank you for holding this public hearing to discuss strategies to increase self-identification by New York City Veterans. My name is Ashton Stewart, I am a Navy Veteran who served in the Gulf War and currently serving as Veterans Program Manager for the MJHS Health System. As a non-Veteran Service Organization, MJHS offers a unique perspective, having overcome the challenge of Veterans not self-identifying by using an effective military assessment tool.

The biggest hurdle to self-identification by Veterans is trust. Only 25% of Veterans are enrolled in the VA and many are unaware that they are eligible for services that can improve their overall wellbeing. As a healthcare provider, MJHS builds trust with Veterans with our comprehensive Military Assessment. This tool has helped us identify those who served by avoiding asking the question, “are you a Veteran.” The identity of “Veteran” is perhaps part of the reason self-identification is so challenging. Simply trying to obtain a “yes” or “no” response for Veteran status does nothing to earn trust from an individual whose time in military service may have been traumatic. The first question asked in the MJHS Military Assessment is, “Did you (or your spouse or family member) serve in the military?” This modified method of identifying Veterans opens dialogue with the patient, because it usually is followed by an explanation by the patient. For example, “Yes, I served, and so did my, spouse, child, father, mother, etc.” Our assessment also includes an open-ended question asking how one view’s their experience in military service, further building upon trust between the clinician and patient. This question can also lead to discovering more about their service and leans into our commitment to providing individualized traumainformed care. The final question asks if the individual would like to speak with someone about services that they may be entitled to, and this is where our Veteran program stands apart.

As a certified Veteran Service Officer, once I connect with a Veteran receiving hospice care, I empower them with eligibility information for services they may be entitled to. We have seen how helpful this knowledge can be to a family in crisis when we are successful placing supportive Veteran services. I often enroll Veterans in the VA for the first time and assist with last-minute service-connected disability applications with the VBA. Enrollment in the VA leads to additional supportive services to compliment MJHS services already in place. This can be a real game changer and provide relief during a stressful time. With the passage of the Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxins (PACT) Act of 2022, more Veterans particularly those who served during the Vietnam Era and the Gulf Wars are eligible to apply for a veteran service-connected disability. Unfortunately, many Veterans we encounter are not aware they qualify when they reach our hospice program. Despite a short timeline to put a claim together, MJHS has been successful with several claims that have been awarded to Veterans or substituted to their surviving

spouse through the DIC (Dependency and Indemnity Compensation) benefit. The challenge is empowering eligible Veterans sooner to apply for these earned benefits, certainly before they need hospice services.

The awareness about available benefits, especially end-of-life benefits, are unknown to most Veterans and their families that we encounter. MJHS empowered over 80 Veterans and their families about burial benefits, and most did not know they were eligible. To foster awareness and understanding among Veterans and their families, MJHS produced a Veteran Resource Guide that provides details to eligibility requirements for services and benefits and how to access them. There is a great educational need within the Veteran community to understand more about know about these benefits. Given the unmet need, MJHS provides this resource not only with our patients, but also through our community outreach. The resources are well received, and we encourage all agencies that we engage with to share this guide with Veterans they serve in addition to implementing a Military Assessment tool. We also encourage other community-based organizations hire a Veteran liaison to help guide similar supportive services to the MJHS program for Veterans and their families.

The MJHS Vet-to-Vet Café is another way that we connect with the community to share vital information about supporting Veterans and their families. We have had robust engagement with the public through our Cafés that emphasize storytelling, sharing of resources, and community building. Our last Café focused on the power of community in improving mental health for Veterans and their families while earlier sessions addressed everything from realities shared by caregivers, medical nexus letters, and the power of music therapy. These resources are recorded and shared on the MJHS YouTube Channel.

Given the rising number of Veterans who need MJHS services and the magnitude of their needs, we are in the process of expanding our Veteran program to include any Veteran under our care—whether the Veterans has come to us for short- or long-term services. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, by 2036, the population of Americans over 65 will increase by 34 percent, while the number of Americans who are 75 and older will increase by 55 percent.1 Many of these individuals are Veterans, or married to a Veteran, and many reside here in New York City. In 2020, it was reported that over 70 percent of New York City Veterans are over the age of 65, highlighting the urgency of our work.2

In 2023, we experienced a 46 percent increase in Veterans and their spouse’s seeking hospice and palliative care compared to 2022. This demand continues to surge with an increase of 15 percent in 2024. We continue to see higher numbers of Vietnam War Veterans who are not service connected but should be. As a city we need to do better at identifying Veterans sooner, before they reach hospice. Perhaps earlier intervention will result in more services that benefit the Veteran and result in a longer life. The need to better equip clinicians is staggering as seen in a study conducted by the RAND Corporation in 2018, Assessing the Capacity of New York State Health Care Providers to Meet the Needs of Veterans. This study showed “only 2.3 percent of health care providers in New York State meet all criteria for

1 Zucker, Howard, M. D. “Where Have all the Doctors Gone?” AARP Bulletin, Jan/Feb 2025, Vol 65 No 1

2 Murphy, Jarrett. "A Statistical Snapshot of NYC's Veterans." City Limits, 11, Nov. 2020, https://citylimits.org/2020/11/11/a-statistical-snapshot-of-nycs-Veterans/.

effectively serving the Veteran population.” Part of the reason for this shocking statistic is generally clinicians do not know how to connect with those who served and are unaware about available supportive services.

To help overcome the challenge of Veterans not self-identifying, MJHS would encourage agencies to implement a Military Assessment, and create a tracking mechanism to measure this tools efficacy. Many organizations do not ask if an individual served in the military, they simply need the motivation to know why it is so important. When we present in the clinician community many are empowered for the first time with information about services and benefits available to Veterans and they genuinely want to help. We share the necessary resources and tools with the hope that they will be implemented. We remind them that once a Military Assessment is agreed upon within their agency, it is important to ask every individual they encounter, “did you or a member of your family serve?” across all services and all departments where services are offered. We don’t want to see Veterans continue to slip through the cracks. Having a Military Assessment in place will help build trust from Veterans by showing them that you care about this important piece of their history, and it will improve the number of Veterans selfidentifying. Further development can take place within an agency by adding a Veteran liaison, or better yet, a certified Veteran Service Officer to help place Veterans on a path to services that can help improve their quality of life.

Thank you to Chair Holden, members of the New York City Committee on Veterans for addressing the issue of Veterans not self-identifying. Please know that MJHS stands at the ready to support your efforts to help Veterans access needed services to improve their overall wellbeing.

Respectfully submitted,

Ashton Stewart Veteran Program Manager

Testimony of Derek Coy Senior Program Officer, Veterans’ Health New York Health Foundation New York City Council Committee on Veterans Oversight – Increasing Self-Identification by New York City Veterans June 10, 2025 Thank you for the opportunity to testify on behalf of the New York Health Foundation (NYHealth) regarding self-identification among veterans. NYHealth is a private, independent, statewide foundation dedicated to improving the health of all New Yorkers, including more than 133,000 veterans who call New York City home. My name is Derek Coy; I’m a Senior Program Officer at NYHealth and a proud veteran, having served as a Sergeant in the United States Marine Corps. NYHealth’s work has consistently highlighted the health-related needs of New York’s veteran population, and one of the most persistent barriers to meeting those needs is how we identify— and fail to identify—veterans across service systems. When it comes to identifying veterans, too often we lead with the question: “Are you a veteran?” That may seem straightforward, but for many, it’s a barrier. Women, LGBTQ+ individuals, people of color, those who served during peacetime, and outside of combat zones or in non-traditional roles often don’t see themselves reflected in that label. Others may have been discharged under other-than-honorable conditions or carry stigma around their service. To address this, we urge New York City to adopt a more inclusive and effective screening question—one that opens the door to care: “Have you or a family member served in the U.S. military?” We know from various state departments of veterans’ services “ask the question” campaigns as well as the U.S. Department of Veterans’ Affairs that how we ask the question matters.1 Veterans do not all look the same or identify in the same way. Critically, this question also captures caregivers and family members, many of whom play an essential role in a veteran’s care and may qualify for support services themselves.
1 “About.” Ask the Question. Accessed June 3, 2025. https://www.askthequestion.nh.gov/about.

Effective identification is not just a best practice—it’s a public health imperative. The consequences of failing to identify veterans are significant: • NYHealth’s recent analysis shows that veterans in New York City die by suicide at roughly twice the rate of civilians.2 • A 2023 RAND study, supported by NYHealth, found more than one-third of New York’s recently transitioned veterans didn’t know what services they were eligible for, and about one in four said they didn’t know where to go to access them.3 When we fail to identify someone as having served, we delay their access to health care, housing, mental health treatment, and suicide prevention services—many of which they earned through their service. When we fail to ask the right question, we fail to connect people with the care they’ve earned. Currently, veteran identification practices vary widely across City agencies and community organizations. This inconsistency leads to inequitable access and weakens the impact of policies and programs intended to support veterans. Although some New York State agencies have begun adopting more inclusive veteran identification questions, broader implementation—particularly in New York City—remains fragmented and incomplete. We recommend the City Council support the following actions: 1. Adopt the use of inclusive veteran identification language. “Have you or a family member served in the U.S. military?” – across all City agency intake forms, service portals, and contracted provider systems. 2. Incentivize and encourage adoption of this screening question in the private sector. This may include health centers, hospitals, housing providers, crisis response, workforce agencies, and legal intake settings. 3. Train frontline staff across sectors. This helps to ensure staff understand who may count as a veteran, why identification matters, and how to make appropriate referrals. This isn’t just about better data—it’s about recognizing the diversity of the veteran community, building trust, improving health outcomes, and ensuring that no veteran or family member goes unrecognized or unsupported in the city they call home.

PREFACE

This book is intended to assist Veterans’ advocates in understanding New York State’s laws that are directly applicable to Veterans, Service Members, and their families. This book is NOT intended to answer every question about every statute and court case impacting this population, but offers instead a thorough first look into this fascinating area of law.

The laws in this book are annotated to assist the reader in understanding the legal interpretations of these statutes. Court Cases and General Counsel Opinions are binding on the implementation and scope of the law within their jurisdiction. Where applicable, we have added the legislative intent to help the reader understand the purposes and goals of the Legislature in the construction of the law. This type of information can be very valuable in advocating for your client. The book uses [brackets] to enclose words added by other than the original drafters to help clarify the meaning or to clearly identify the topic of the law.

Please take notice of the effective date of this publication. The law changes as often as the tides, and is relevant and binding only in its most recent incarnation.

If there is a question regarding any law referenced in this book, please contact the General Counsel of the New York State Department of Veterans’ Services.

Such report shall include, but not be limited to, the following information to the extent it is reasonably accessible to the department: (a) an analysis of veterans in New York state who are currently homeless, or have been homeless within five years of being released from active duty including an analysis of gender as it relates to homelessness of veterans; (b) data on the number of children of homeless veterans, including the current placement of such children; (c) cases of military sexual trauma experienced by homeless veterans while on active duty or during military training, including a breakdown of the collected data based upon the gender of the victim; and (d) the unemployment rate for New York state veterans. The term “children of homeless veterans” shall mean a person who is unmarried and who is under the age of eighteen years, and is the biological or legally adopted child of a veteran. The report shall be delivered to the governor, the speaker of the assembly and the temporary president of the senate by June thirtieth, two thousand twenty and every three years thereafter. Such report shall be publicly available and posted on the department of veterans’ services website.
